subject: 🚙 U.S., China change lanes

Plus: OpenAI's latest departure | Thursday, August 13, 2026

Axios Closer
By Nathan Bomey · Aug 13, 2026

Thursday ✅.

Today's newsletter is 809 words, a 3-minute read.

📈 The dashboard: The S&P 500 closed up 0.7%, hitting a new record high.

  • There was more evidence of cooling inflation today, with producer prices flat in July.

🥶 Today's stock spotlight: Cisco Systems (-8.4%), the networking equipment giant, delivered better-than-expected earnings, but an underwhelming outlook disappointed investors.

 
 
1 big thing: Changing lanes
 

Illustration: Allie Carl/Axios

 

The U.S. auto industry's retreat from China is accelerating, while Chinese carmakers are inching closer to the American market despite attempts to keep them out.

Why it matters: China once represented a lucrative growth opportunity and manufacturing base for American automakers, but those ties are unraveling as Chinese rivals like BYD and Geely expand their reach around the world.

The latest: Ford announced late yesterday that it will end production of its Lincoln luxury brand in China for export to the U.S., while General Motors is reportedly ceasing sales of its Chevrolet brand in China.

  • Ford said it'll expand production in the U.S., where it currently makes Lincoln vehicles in Louisville and Chicago.
  • GM will focus on Buick and Cadillac sales in China, and will continue to build Chevys there for export elsewhere.

State of play: Chinese vehicles are catching up on quality, and with excess production capacity, the country's automakers have been engaged in a feverish price war, undercutting the competition around the world.

Meanwhile, the path for Chinese vehicles to reach the U.S. market looks like it'll initially run through North American production rather than exports from China, Tu Le, founder of Detroit-area consultancy Sino Auto Insights, tells Axios.

  • That could involve standing up plants in Mexico, though the Trump administration today released a report assailing Mexico as one of "China's biggest enablers" for allowing China to build what it called "shadow transshipment networks" designed to evade U.S. tariffs — a beef that potentially complicates that route.

The intrigue: It could become smoother, however, if Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum gets her way.

  • "The Mexican government is pushing the U.S. to lower tariffs on North American automobiles as part of conversations over reworking the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement," WSJ reported.

2. OpenAI latest departure
 

Illustration: Natalie Peeples/Axios

 

OpenAI chief revenue officer Denise Dresser is leaving the company less than a year into the role, Axios' Madison Mills writes.

Why it matters: It's the latest in a series of recent executive departures for the AI company.

  • The announcement comes just days after the exit of longtime exec Brad Lightcap.
  • Fidji Simo, OpenAI's head of product and business, left her role at the company last month due to a chronic illness.
  • Dresser had been tasked with filling in for both — when Lightcap was moved out of the COO role and Simo took medical leave.

State of play: OpenAI has appointed Dali Rajic, most recently president and COO of Google-owned cybersecurity company Wiz, to replace Dresser.

The big picture: The moves come as co-founder Greg Brockman consolidates more operating responsibility around himself while OpenAI grows its enterprise business to prepare to go public.

 
 
3. Other happenings
 

Shipping cargo containers at the Port of Long Beach. Photo: Bob Riha, Jr./Getty Images

 

🏷️ A federal trade court ruled that President Trump can block cheap imports — including from Chinese retailers like Temu and Shein — from entering the U.S. tariff-free. (Axios)

🤖 Anthropic reportedly is in talks to buy Decart, a developer of world models and chip optimization software, for around $6 billion. (Axios)

🥩 Tyson Foods plans to close multiple beef plants as it grapples with a global shortage of cattle that has jolted prices and undermined profits. (Bloomberg)

4. Color fade
 

Food companies are under pressure to remove artificial colors from their food. Photo: Kevin Carter/Getty Images

 

The quickest way for food companies to alleviate pressure to ditch artificial colors in their products might be to just ditch colors entirely.

State of play: Makers of products like freezer pops and sports drinks may remove colors altogether as they face pressure from the Trump administration and the MAHA movement to remove synthetic dyes, Bloomberg reports.

  • Part of the concern is that the natural ingredients have a shorter shelf life and "are likely to get more expensive as more of the industry reaches for them."

🎨 Yes, but: Not everyone is ready to give up on colors.

  • Mars has about 100 employees working on its plan to eliminate artificial colors from M&Ms — with about a quarter solely dedicated to trying to replicate the color blue with natural ingredients, WSJ reported in June.

💭 Nathan's thought bubble: I wonder whether this push will fade if and when RFK leaves the administration.

🗓️ On this day in 1913, metallurgist Harry Brearley somewhat unintentionally invented stainless steel. Working for Brown Firth Research Lab in the U.K. on behalf of a client pursuing an erosion-resistant gun barrel, he produced an alloy that didn't seem to corrode. His "rustless steel" didn't do much for the gun manufacturer, but a local cutlery maker was interested — and changed the name to the more appetizing "stainless steel."
